Good morning, members of the committee. My name is Leslie Anderson. I am the Director of Planning and Development for the City of Saskatoon, and I am here today to present on the Saskatoon Homelessness Action Plan. The city has been collaborating since 2024 with community partners to develop this community plan. This has included an executive group with representatives from Saskatoon Tribal Council, Métis Nations Saskatchewan, and Saskatoon Housing Initiatives Partnership, along with the city. In addition to this group, there has also been a larger community advisory group with representatives from over 20 community organizations involved in the response and support to those experiencing homelessness.

In mid-2025, City Council received a report outlining roles for the city in implementing this plan. Actions were identified as aligning with the city's jurisdiction and our abilities, and we received direction to take on a leadership role in those specific actions last summer. Since last year, the SHAP Executive Council has been working to incorporate additional elements into the plan, including data, key performance indicators, as well as monitoring and reporting mechanisms to support the implementation and accountability for the plan. The plan identifies strategic priorities to guide action in the community, including increasing the supply of affordable, supportive, and transitional housing, addressing systemic barriers to reduce the inflows into homelessness, and strengthening collaboration and coordination across sectors.

As we reported last year, the city's proposed implementation role includes coordinating with partners across sectors and jurisdictions, supporting system planning and alignment, affordable housing and land use support, advocacy and partnership building, monitoring progress against the key performance indicators, and reporting to City Council, the Executive Council, and community partners on implementation status and outcomes. Many of the actions to be led by the city are aligned with existing initiatives that we already have in place, including several which have already received approved funding from City Council, such as the Affordable Housing Strategy. While other actions may require future budget requests to move forward, those specific municipal budget requirements would be further refined as we move into implementation and will be brought forward for any specific consideration or approval required by City Council at the appropriate time.

Today, we are presenting the final community plan for information and asking for City Council to reaffirm the city's role in the plan, consistent with what was approved last year. Administration will then continue to work with partners to advance the implementation and bring forward items for further review and approval as required, while continuing to refine the roles, the timelines, and the resource requirements to support the plan. With that, I know there are several speakers, and I can address any questions when required.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Good morning, my name is Karen Colbison. I am the CEO of the Saskatoon West Business Association. I have been researching and analyzing Saskatoon's available homelessness data for just about 14 years, and I come before you today to tell you that, as you just heard, this report is not a novel approach; it is simply history repeated.

The Saskatoon United Way conducted Saskatoon's first point-in-time counts in 2008, with subsequent counts in 2012 and 2014. At that time, the recommendations to end homelessness were increasing the number of affordable housing units, making the waitlist application process less difficult, reducing barriers, and partnering and collaborating with community agencies. In November of 2016, the Saskatoon Community Entity delivered a new homelessness action plan to City Council, which was a five-year strategy developed by a community steering committee. It focused on, and I quote, "increasing affordable and transitional housing supply, reducing barriers, and coordinating community support services to address homelessness."

In 2025, the action plan today highlights three priority areas: increasing affordable housing supply, addressing systemic barriers to reduce inflows into homelessness, and increasing support and community collaboration. In 2012, 2014, 2016, and 2025, Saskatoon's homelessness action plans have never changed, and they have not produced measurable results. I think to better understand why we have not produced measurable reductions in homelessness, we really need to look no further than the funding model.

From 2012 through 2024, Saskatoon community-based organizations received just over $40 million in funding, just from the Reaching Home federal government program alone. Of that $40 million, $28.2 million was received between 2022 and 2024. Over 70% of the funding came in just two years, and during that exact same time period, we recorded a 170% increase in homelessness in our city. This is the highest increase on record, dating back to 2008. I think the parallel is undeniable, and across Canada, the results are the same: more funding, yet we have more homelessness.

How was the money spent? Of that $40 million, 45% went to agency staffing and administration. 36% went to programming, such as meals, ID clinics, etc., and 12% went to service providers' facility maintenance and upgrades. That is over nine out of every ten dollars spent on serving homelessness, not solving it. It is an uncomfortable paradox: organizations are funded to eradicate the very problem that extends their existence. This leads to a zero-sum game where the homelessness-serving sector sustains jobs and careers, but it equally fails to sustain the lives of those unhoused.

To be clear, this is not a frontline problem; it is a system design and policy failure problem. Every outreach worker, shelter support, and case manager is deeply compassionate. The history lesson today should serve as a wake-up call. If we continue with essentially the same plan we have had for 14-plus years, it will never resolve homelessness, because it is literally, financially, and mathematically impossible. There are solutions, though. Proof-of-concept projects are being implemented in over 100 jurisdictions across North America, with 84 of those indicating successful reductions in homelessness at a population level, meaning outflow is exceeding inflow. That is the single standard of measurement upon which success is achieved. The solution is not more money; it is smarter money. For today, as you receive this information and approve this report, I would encourage you to think differently about the entire system. I would encourage you to ask yourself if you believe we are truly making an impact on unhoused people despite record levels of financial investment and plans that never materialize into results. I would also encourage you to ask the communities you represent and the residents you serve if they believe that what we are doing is currently working. So we have three options. One, we can do nothing. Two, we can do more of the same. Or three, we can do something different. I believe we can end homelessness in Saskatoon with strategy, measurement, and actual numbers that reduce inflow and exceed in outflow. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Colison. Yes, we have some questions from Council. We'll start with Councillor Pearce.
Councillor Pearce: Thank you, Madam Chair. I know, Ms. Colison, you've studied this a long time and we've had a couple of conversations. I'm really interested in your take. I noticed in Ontario and a couple other places they are bold and saying they want to end homelessness. I know you've studied this. Do you have any recommendations from your perspective that would actually help us end homelessness?
Ms. Colison: Thank you. Thank you for the question, Madam Chair. The key component, we can even look at Regina; they have also just released their homelessness action plan. The number one thing is measurement. Point-in-time counts are anecdotal; they wildly fluctuate. Everyone here, even the people speaking today, will agree that point-in-time counts capture a snapshot of homelessness. So we need quality by-name data. The 100 communities I talked about, that is where they are. We have by-name data, but it is not sufficient enough to qualify what the needs are. So we can sit here and say, 'housing first' or 'we need these support services,' and we do need addiction treatment and all those things. But right now, what we're doing is upside down because we're not responding to the needs based on the anecdotal data we have. So, quality by-name measurement is the first step in how we need to get through this. And that's a big undertaking. Thank you.

Mayor Block: Thank you, Chair Parker, and thank you for being here, Ms. Colison, and for doing a lot of work on this so we can have a robust discussion today. Could you just tell me a little bit more about what 'quality by-name data' means? What do you need in order to have that?
Ms. Colison: So, we currently use HIFIS and coordinated access. But there are a couple of problems, and this is not something I'm sure the city can work towards, but it's a bigger conversation. Basically, those are not mandated. Neither participation in HIFIS nor participation in coordinated access, which is the shared servicing, is mandated. So, for example, if someone is unhoused and they go to a Friendship Centre for lunch, they should be identified as an individual. 'How are you today?' And maybe they went to White Buffalo the day before. The quality by-name data captures that person's health needs, what barriers they've been through. 'Do you want housing?' 'No.' 'Okay, great.' We'll put them on an active list and we'll work for people that are active in the system. So the quality by-name data indicates health needs, housing needs, and support needed, if any. Maybe it's just income, right? So we take the numbers that we have; they are actually put into a system. And then that system is shared amongst all service providers, which sort of is now, but it's not mandated, and that's the difference. And then we can really address; we can see trends. We can address the immediate needs of people who just need housing, or the immediate needs of people who just need to go to a detox or treatment center, right? As opposed to 'building it and they will come,' they come and then we build it. I guess that's how I would explain it.
Mayor Block: Okay. So I think what I'm hearing you say is that the ability to have that kind of data exists, but it just isn't mandated. And so, it's not necessarily... I won't get into whether or not the province is sharing all of those questions of our administration. But I am interested if you could just elaborate a little bit further about what you're seeing for success in other cities and what that is, exactly.
Ms. Colison: I'll give you a really good example. So you may or may not know, I was recently at a HUMA parliamentary committee, the study on homelessness in Canada. And while there, I had the good fortune to meet a fellow from St. Catharines who runs a youth shelter, or I should say, he ran a youth shelter for his organization. And over time—it's taken about three years—they realized that for every youth that they found successful placement for, whether that was simply returning home or whatever the case may be, for every one youth they found success for, there were two coming in. And there was probably more, but it was two to one, two to one. So that was turning their whole system upside down, creating backlogs and inefficiencies. So they decided to address the needs with this quality by-name data of these youth. I won't go into all the complete details of it, but essentially, his testimony at HUMA was that they actually ended up closing one of their two shelters because they were able to be so successful in prevention and diversion that they did not need the second shelter. I think they went from 68 beds to maybe like 28, or something like it was less than half. But what they did was, without loss of funding, they shifted their priorities and their working model from simply sheltering people to prevention and diversion, and that took time. But they ended up closing a whole youth shelter as a result of that shift, and the outflow then exceeded their inflow. That's the goal. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Next on the list, we have Matthew Gooday. Great. Welcome, Matthew. I know you've been here before. You've got five minutes. Good morning. Your Worship, members of the committee, thanks for having me. My name is Matthew Goodet. I'm the Director of Housing and Homelessness, and I'm here today on behalf of the Métis Nation–Saskatchewan to endorse the Saskatoon Homelessness Action Plan and future requests that arise from it. As part of the Executive Council, I valued my time working alongside the city's housing team, Saskatoon Initiatives Partnership, and numerous community partners to establish a coordinated approach to addressing unprecedented homelessness in our city. I'll be the first to admit that the development of this plan was not an easy task. Homelessness is a complex issue influenced by a wide range of personal, social, and economic factors. While many of those factors could each require their own dedicated strategy, we chose to focus on housing and homelessness responses. Developing this plan required more than technical expertise; it required collaboration, trust, and a willingness to find common ground among more than 30 organizations with different mandates, perspectives, and priorities. At times, that seemed like an impossible task, but through consistent dialogue and a shared commitment to improving outcomes for people experiencing homelessness, we reached consensus on a coordinated path forward. The result is a community-driven plan built around three key priorities: Number one, increasing affordable housing supply; Number two, addressing systemic barriers to reduce the inflows into homelessness; Number three, increasing and supporting community collaboration. Also, importantly, embedded throughout the plan is the inclusion of Indigenous leadership and culturally appropriate responses, recognizing the disproportionate impacts of homelessness on Indigenous peoples in Saskatoon. Within each of these key priorities are a number of action and sub-action items that I hope will help the city, the provincial government, the federal government, Indigenous governments, community-based organizations, and even the private sector focus their efforts and resources to make a greater overall impact. What makes this plan particularly valuable is that it's not intended to sit on a shelf. It is a practical framework that organizations can use to guide investments, policy decisions, advocacy efforts, and program development. I'll be the first to acknowledge that this plan is not perfect, and it's certainly not going to end homelessness on its own. Homelessness is far too complex for any single plan to solve. What it provides is a tool towards shared focus and a foundation for meaningful collaboration. By focusing on the same priorities, we can make faster decisions, reduce duplication, and ensure our efforts complement one another rather than competing for the same resources. Some of this alignment is already in action. I've actually stood up here a couple of times this past year in support of the city's affordable housing strategy and the development of the land acquisition and disposition policy, both examples of work being done in response to efforts from the ShAP. Additionally, these are not just future aspirations. M&S is already using priorities identified in ShAP to inform our own investments in initiatives. We are increasing our focus on supportive and transitional housing with the construction of a 16-unit supportive housing complex in Kensington. We also recently invested over $2 million in distinctions-based urban homelessness strategies, including partnering with the city towards the company's washroom project. M&S continues to work and advocate for the expansion of coordinated access and is actively working on enhancing data collection and analysis, including working with the University of Saskatchewan on research and creating a systems map with ShAP. A recent proposal to build "kind of homes" is heavily focused on aligned priorities, including a 54-unit affordable housing complex and a 24-unit supportive housing complex for high-acuity families. These examples show that the plan is already doing what it was meant to do, helping us align our work and move toward action. Just as importantly, they reflect the relationships and collaboration we have built over the past year, something that I am proud to be a part of and hope continues to grow. The city has played a critical leadership role throughout the development of this plan and will continue to play an important role in its implementation, requiring future budget requests, policy decisions, and other efforts. But I guess you can see this as us having already done some of the legwork for you. We spent the last year gathering input and collaborating with the community to develop action plans and priorities, as well as key performance indicators for monitoring and evaluation. We now have a shared vision, we have a roadmap. We have organizations already aligning their investments and efforts around these priorities. What we need now is continued leadership and commitment to implementation. I encourage Council to endorse the ShAP and continue supporting the investments, policy decisions, and collaborative efforts. We need to turn this vision into measurable results for the people who need it most. On behalf of M&S, I would like to thank City Administration, SHIP, Saskatoon Tribal Council, and our community partners, elders, and those who have lived experience who have contributed to this work. We look forward to continuing this journey together. Marci, thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Do we have any questions from committee? Okay, not seeing any, I do have one question. Just because you're part of the executive committee that has helped put this together, you've been quite involved. Part of our next steps are defining roles, creating or identifying priority actions, and creating timelines. Are there any concerns that the city endorsed what our role was sometime ago, and now we have the ShAP sitting in front of us, which is great? But now we have this next step. We don't have to wait on; M&S has started, and I know administration has started on some of these priorities as well. But are there any concerns that this report almost is missing that last piece from the group that's put the ShAP together? The plan is there, but the plan feels a little bit unfinished. Are there any concerns? That's what I alluded to when I was saying that it's not perfect on the implementation side. I'll admit it could be more robust. However, we struggled with that one because it's tough to know who and how to implement all these actions when you don't know the resources involved yet. You don't know who will have those resources, and you're not sure who's committed yet to working on all of those. So that's why I'm aligning it as a tool and a road map. I know the city has stepped up as a leadership role for the implementation of it, and the executive council will continue to help with that as well, and monitor and evaluate it. But unfortunately, it's not as easy as just "you do this, you do that, you do this." I wish it was. So one of the pieces is that there needs to be a bit of a reiterative review. As you said, funding changes, priorities change, and what groups are able to do or have capacity for changes. Do you have any recommendations on what that cycle of that reiterative review should look like? How often should we be taking a look at this? I think the city and the executive council should be reviewing it quarterly at a minimum. But I think that this plan should be reviewed annually and should be updated every three to four years. We've learned some lessons on doing this, and we have some suggestions on how we can improve it going forward. So, let's not just make this the last one. Let's keep improving on it and learn from those lessons and continue working. Part of the beauty of creating this wasn't just what came out of it, but it was the relationships built in the collaboration that was built as part of creating it. So it forced us all to get together and talk about it together, and I think that's important that we should continue doing that. Okay, great. Thank you very much. All right. On to our next speaker, we have Gordon Taylor. Again, Mr. Taylor, you've been here before; you know how it all works. Please introduce yourself and begin when you're ready. Thank you. Good morning, friends. It's great to be here. My name is Major Gordon Taylor, the executive director at the Salvation Army, and I want to start by saying thank you so much for the opportunity to speak into this today. It's a privilege I never take lightly, and I'm always thankful to live in a country and in a city where we have the chance to participate in this way when it comes to public policy. I also want to start by acknowledging that while I'm happy that this action plan is being presented today and that it's hopefully going to be passed and prompting more action to be taken, it's also true that action is taken every day in our community by those who are working on the front lines and providing help to those who are homeless and in need. I want to acknowledge the incredible work that's done by our colleagues and partners in this sector on a daily basis. There are two items in the action plan that I want to add an exclamation mark to, as I see them as very key and important. First is item 1.1, where it talks about the importance of affordable housing, but there's a second line to that that says, "with a focus on transitional and supportive housing." In the entire housing continuum, I think this is an incredibly key piece that needs a lot of emphasis. It's not enough to have market housing that's affordable available to people who need housing. We have a lot of people in our community who are a part of that pit count who aren't ready for that. They're not ready to successfully be housed in market housing; they need a transitional along the continuum preparing for that. So, more transitional and supportive housing, I think, is a key element to making this whole plan go forward. And one of the missing pieces in all of that is funding for transitional and supportive housing. It's very difficult to find operational funding for any of us who are operating those types of places in order to operate them. There are a couple of transitional housing places in town, and there's no funding for them at this point in time. We would love to duplicate them; we can afford to do a couple, we're losing money, but we can't do 10. So that's a key point. One of the other points I want to underscore and emphasize is one that I've been talking about for the last three years, sometimes from this podium, and that is item 2.2 in the plan, where it's discussing the need for a basic shelter. I'm glad that it's in the plan and still seen as a need, but what I've seen as being the trend over the last couple of years is more of an emphasis on having drop-in and overnight warming centers and solving the need for basic shelter in those other ways that is not as good. An overnight warming center, like the one we've operated at St. Mary's Church the last three winters, allows us to get people in out of the cold and save them from freezing to death. It's a harm reduction approach because there's nothing else there, and it's needed because we don't have anything better in place. We're not allowed to have beds or cots or mats on the floor; it's the place to come in and warm up. There's a big open hall with people all over the place, and there's no dignity for them, and it's almost impossible to get a proper night's sleep, and they're not even supposed to sleep in that space. A basic shelter provides beds, provides showers, provides a much better alternative to that, provides the dignity and the opportunity when you're staying at a basic shelter each night for a while. To start to feel better, to be healthier, and then better to start to move forward in the continuum to then maybe to an enhanced shelter, and then to supportive housing, and then continue to move forward. But the model we have right now is missing that very important piece, and from what I've seen, because I know how much we're funded the last couple of winters to operate the overnight warming center and having a couple of those in town, one for men and one for women, that doesn't cost more than what a basic shelter costs. So the basic shelter would be a much better model to move to, with the challenges of where do you put it, what kind of building do you use, but I think it's very important that we look at that as an important piece. The final thing I want to mention is something I've also mentioned before: when we're moving forward providing needed services, and we still do need shelters, we need to be very careful not to put large overnight locations next door to each other on the same block. I've seen that problem in many places, and it's been commented on by our national safety advisor that the cities he's addressing the most problems in are the cities where everything's in one neighborhood. Thank you, Mr. Taylor, I appreciate your comments. Do we have some questions? Yes, we can. Councillor Kelleher, please go first. Thank you, and through you, Madam Chair. Mr. Taylor, could you speak a little bit to the difference between a basic shelter and an enhanced shelter, just so we're all level set on that? And then, could you comment a little bit on where you see the barriers to establishing that are in the city, just from your perspective?

I have a question. It's a question that comes up quite often: the difference between the different types of shelters that the province currently funds. In Saskatoon, we have three enhanced shelters: ourselves, the Mustard Seed, and STC. We all have the same contract for an enhanced shelter. People are staying there 24 hours a day, get three meals a day, and are during this stay required to be involved in case-managed work, case management working towards being housed. They're quite well funded. The expectations are to show results, and we're doing that quite successfully, helping people move through the continuum onto those next steps when there's housing available. That's an enhanced shelter, 24/7 being one of the key pieces. A basic shelter is one that is funded to operate overnight to give someone a safe, good place to sleep for the night with showers and all the rest of it, and they get breakfast in the morning and then they're out for the day. To me, the missing piece that you can add on if we had a large basic shelter in town is once you have that building established. During the daytime, when the shelter portion is closed, it could also be the hub for providing other services in the same building. Just because the shelter contract only pays for the overnight doesn't mean we couldn't also use the space in some other way during the day. That basic shelter piece is key, I think, and very much missing. I can't remember your second question, sorry.

To get us all on the same page about what a basic shelter is, what do you see as the main barriers to having one?

I've had a lot of conversations with our actual funder about this, and we really see basic shelter pieces as a key thing that's needed. The answer I get back from them is that a basic shelter would only be funded if the city asks for it. They're not going to listen to me; you need to ask for it.

Thank you. From your experience, and given that the Salvation Army has projects across the country, are there other areas you could speak to where there are basic shelters and enhanced shelters, and are clients moving through the continuum? In your general opinion, or any anecdotal pieces that you may have, is it better than what they may be in Saskatoon?

Most of my experience I can speak to would just be where I was prior to here, in Winnipeg. I'm not sure what happens in other provinces; every province has different funding models and different definitions, so it's hard to compare. I know in Winnipeg, the center I was in charge of there, we had emergency shelter and transitional housing in the same location, which made it work a lot better for us for moving people through the continuum. It was a very large facility, 400 beds, and the problem there was that the other three large facilities doing similar work were all within a block of us, and the neighbor was just a disaster.

Okay, those are my questions. Thank you.

Okay, Councillor Pearce, your thanks.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for those explanations. I want to ask you: with enhanced shelters housing somebody 24 hours a day, working towards being housed, how many of your residents are working towards that, and what is your success rate in seeing them placed?

As far as the number of residents working towards that, I'll give a little bit more explanation on how the contract works. If someone comes and just needs a bed for the night, they can be booked in and get a bed. They're required after a couple of days to then start to see a caseworker and work. If they refuse to, because not everyone wants to or is ready to, there's a limit of how long they can stay: 10 days. But if they are engaged in participating in that work, they can then stay for 30 days. And if at that 30-day mark they're still working, but just haven't found a place yet, then it can be renewed. The length of stay is based on their participation with our case management team in being housed. Part of our case management team on site, we have our own full-time caseworkers. Also, an intake worker from the Ministry of Social Services has an office in our building as well, so they're working together as a team. That's a great model that works well. I don't have the numbers with me as far as the success rate, but I know that our funder is happy, and so are we, with how things are going. But the exact numbers I don't have at the top of my head.

Okay, and I'm going to pose the same question to you that I posed to Miss Colbus: what would you see as things that need to happen in order to actually start reducing and looking to functionally end homelessness in the province or even in our city?

We just need to fill those gaps in the continuum, and unfortunately, there are gaps at almost every step of the way. For someone who's completely sleeping rough, if you want to put it that way, and has nowhere to be that night, their first step into the continuum most often will be into a basic shelter, if we had one. Right now, in the winter months, it's into one of the overnight warming centers, and in the summer, it seems to be into encampments.
